claim: Animal behavior is regulated based on the values of future rewards.
source: Animal behavior is regulated based on the values of future rewards.
evidence: This is a general statement about behavioral regulation that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons signals reward values.
source: The phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons signals these values.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: Reward values often change over time on a subsecond-by-subsecond basis.
source: Because reward values often change over time, even on a subsecond-by-subsecond basis, appropriate behavioral regulation requires continuous value monitoring.
evidence: This is presented as a known characteristic of reward values in real-world situations.

claim: Appropriate behavioral regulation requires continuous value monitoring when reward values change over time.
source: Because reward values often change over time, even on a subsecond-by-subsecond basis, appropriate behavioral regulation requires continuous value monitoring.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for behavioral regulation in changing environments.

claim: Phasic dopamine activity is sporadic and has a short duration.
source: However, the phasic dopamine activity, which is sporadic and has a short duration, likely fails continuous monitoring.
evidence: This characterization of phasic dopamine activity is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Phasic dopamine activity likely fails continuous monitoring of changing reward values.
source: However, the phasic dopamine activity, which is sporadic and has a short duration, likely fails continuous monitoring.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the characteristics of phasic activity.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibit a tonic firing mode that effectively tracks changing reward values.
source: Here, we demonstrate a tonic firing mode of dopamine neurons that effectively tracks changing reward values.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dopamine neuron activity was recorded in monkeys during a Pavlovian procedure in which the value of a cued reward gradually increased or decreased.
source: We recorded dopamine neuron activity in monkeys during a Pavlovian procedure in which the value of a cued reward gradually increased or decreased.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Dopamine neurons tonically increased and decreased their activity as the reward value changed.
source: Dopamine neurons tonically increased and decreased their activity as the reward value changed.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tonic dopamine activity was evoked more strongly by non-burst spikes than burst spikes.
source: This tonic activity was evoked more strongly by non-burst spikes than burst spikes producing a conventional phasic activity.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data comparing burst and non-burst spike contributions.

claim: Burst spikes produce conventional phasic dopamine activity.
source: This tonic activity was evoked more strongly by non-burst spikes than burst spikes producing a conventional phasic activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about dopamine neuron firing modes.

claim: Dopamine neurons change their firing mode to effectively signal reward values in a given situation.
source: Our findings suggest that dopamine neurons change their firing mode to effectively signal reward values in a given situation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons respond to rewards and reward-predicting cues with phasic activity.
source: These neurons respond to rewards and reward-predicting cues with phasic activity (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Cohen et al., 2012; Kawagoe et al., 2004; Morris et al., 2004; Satoh et al., 2003; Schultz, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Phasic activity of dopamine neurons represents reward prediction errors in reinforcement learning.
source: An influential theory proposed that such phasic activity of dopamine neurons represents reward prediction errors, discrepancies between obtained and predicted reward values, in reinforcement learning (Doya, 2002; Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997)
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations to influential papers in the field.

claim: Reward prediction errors are discrepancies between obtained and predicted reward values.
source: An influential theory proposed that such phasic activity of dopamine neurons represents reward prediction errors, discrepancies between obtained and predicted reward values, in reinforcement learning (Doya, 2002; Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997)
evidence: This is a definition of reward prediction errors from reinforcement learning theory.

claim: Reward-evoked phasic activity of dopamine neurons regulates reinforcement learning.
source: and the reward-evoked phasic activity of dopamine neurons has been shown to regulate this type of learning (Chang et al., 2016; Stauffer et al., 2016; Steinberg et al., 2013; Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Cue-evoked phasic activity of dopamine neurons reflects the value of cued rewards.
source: In addition, the cue-evoked phasic activity of dopamine neurons has been reported to reflect the value of cued rewards (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Roesch et al., 2007; Tobler et al., 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cue-evoked phasic activity of dopamine neurons influences behavior associated with cued rewards.
source: and has recently been demonstrated to influence behavior associated with cued rewards (Maes et al., 2020; Morrens et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent experimental studies.

claim: Phasic dopamine activity has a duration of around a couple of hundred milliseconds.
source: Indeed, if reward values gradually change moment-by-moment as in the cocktail situation described above, the phasic activity of dopamine neurons, which is sporadic and has a short duration (around a couple of hundred milliseconds), likely fails to continuously track these changing values.
evidence: This is a characterization of phasic dopamine activity based on established knowledge.

claim: Phasic dopamine activity seems unable to properly regulate reward-seeking behavior in changing environments where reward values fluctuate.
source: Therefore, the phasic activity seems to be unable to properly regulate reward-seeking behavior in changing environments in which reward values fluctuate.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the characteristics of phasic activity and the requirements of changing environments.

claim: The study used a Pavlovian procedure in which a visual cue indicated the value of a liquid reward that gradually increased or decreased moment-by-moment.
source: To address whether and how dopamine neurons signal changing reward values, we designed a Pavlovian procedure in which a visual cue indicated the value (i.e., the amount) of a liquid reward that gradually increased or decreased moment-by-moment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Single-unit activity was recorded from dopamine neurons while macaque monkeys were conditioned with the Pavlovian procedure.
source: We recorded single-unit activity from dopamine neurons while macaque monkeys were conditioned with this Pavlovian procedure.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The Pavlovian procedure had three different conditions.
source: We designed a Pavlovian procedure with three different conditions (Figure 1A–C) and applied it to two macaque monkeys (monkey H and monkey P).
evidence: This describes the experimental design as shown in the figures.

claim: The study used two macaque monkeys (monkey H and monkey P).
source: We designed a Pavlovian procedure with three different conditions (Figure 1A–C) and applied it to two macaque monkeys (monkey H and monkey P).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: A bar stimulus with red and green areas was presented as a conditioned stimulus after a fixation period.
source: In each condition, a bar stimulus with red and green areas was presented as a conditioned stimulus (CS) after a fixation period.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The size of the green area indicated the amount of a liquid reward that the monkey would receive.
source: The size of the green area indicated the amount (i.e., the value) of a liquid reward that the monkey would receive.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and how reward value was signaled.

claim: The larger the green area became, the larger the associated reward value.
source: The larger the green area became, the larger the associated reward value.
evidence: This describes the relationship between visual cue and reward value in the experimental design.

claim: In the value-increase condition, the green area was minimal at the beginning and gradually increased at 3.8°/s.
source: In the first condition (value-increase condition, Figure 1A), the green area was minimal at the beginning and gradually increased (3.8°/s), that is, the reward value gradually increased (0.082 ml/s) (Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the value-increase condition, with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: In the value-increase condition, the reward value gradually increased at 0.082 ml/s.
source: In the first condition (value-increase condition, Figure 1A), the green area was minimal at the beginning and gradually increased (3.8°/s), that is, the reward value gradually increased (0.082 ml/s) (Video 1).
evidence: This describes the rate of reward value increase in the experimental design.

claim: In the value-increase condition, the gradual increase randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the onset of the bar stimulus.
source: The gradual increase randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the onset of the bar stimulus.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: In the value-decrease condition, the green area was maximal at the beginning and gradually decreased at 3.8°/s.
source: In the second condition (value-decrease condition, Figure 1B), the green area was maximal at the beginning and gradually decreased (3.8°/s), that is, the reward value gradually decreased (0.082 ml/s) (Video 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the value-decrease condition, with reference to Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: In the value-decrease condition, the reward value gradually decreased at 0.082 ml/s.
source: In the second condition (value-decrease condition, Figure 1B), the green area was maximal at the beginning and gradually decreased (3.8°/s), that is, the reward value gradually decreased (0.082 ml/s) (Video 2).
evidence: This describes the rate of reward value decrease in the experimental design.

claim: In the value-decrease condition, the gradual decrease randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the bar onset.
source: The gradual decrease randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the bar onset.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: In the value-fixed condition, the size of the green area did not change and was fixed at the minimum, half, or maximum predicting 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 ml reward, respectively.
source: In the third condition (value-fixed condition, Figure 1C), the size of the green area did not change and was instead fixed at the minimum, half, or maximum that predicted a 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 ml reward, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the value-fixed condition, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: A CS with a longitudinally halved green area was included and was randomly followed by a 0.1-0.3 ml reward (uncertain reward value).
source: In addition to these CSs, a CS with a longitudinally halved green area was included and was randomly followed by a 0.1-0.3 ml reward (i.e., the reward value was uncertain).
evidence: This describes an additional condition in the experimental design.

claim: The monkeys received the reward indicated by the green area immediately after the offset of the bar stimulus.
source: In each condition, the monkeys received the reward indicated by the green area immediately after the offset of the bar stimulus.
evidence: This describes the timing of reward delivery in the experimental procedure.

claim: The delay between the CS onset and the reward delivery was fixed at 2850 ms in each condition and did not change across trials.
source: The delay between the CS onset and the reward delivery was fixed at 2850 ms in each condition and did not change across trials.
evidence: This describes a controlled parameter in the experimental design.

claim: Each condition consisted of a block of 50 trials and was repeated once or more for each recording session.
source: Each condition consisted of a block of 50 trials and was repeated once or more for each recording session (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the structure of the experimental sessions, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The monkeys were more likely to choose the bar stimulus with the larger green area in the choice task.
source: We observed that the monkeys were more likely to choose the bar stimulus with the larger green area, that is, the logistic regression slope between the choice rate of the right bar stimulus and the value difference (right bar's value – left bar's value) was significantly larger than zero (monkey H: n = 85 sessions, mean ± SD = 0.94 ± 1.64, p=1.17 × 10−15; monkey P: n = 68 sessions, mean ± SD = 0.98 ± 1.65, p=7.64 × 10−13; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The monkeys correctly predicted the reward values according to the size of the green area.
source: This suggests that the monkeys correctly predicted the reward values according to the size of the green area.
evidence: This is an inference based on the choice behavior data.

claim: 99 dopamine neurons were recorded from monkey H (n=46) and monkey P (n=53) in and around the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area.
source: While the monkeys participated in the Pavlovian procedure, we recorded single-unit activity from 99 dopamine neurons (monkey H, n = 46; monkey P, n = 53) in and around the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, also see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for the characteristic spike waveforms of the recorded dopamine neurons).
evidence: This describes the data collection, with references to supplementary figures showing recording locations and spike characteristics.

claim: An example dopamine neuron tonically increased its activity as the reward value gradually increased in the value-increase condition.
source: Indeed, an example dopamine neuron tonically increased its activity as the reward value gradually increased in the value-increase condition (left in Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes an observation from a single neuron example, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The tonic increase in activity was clearly in contrast with the phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition.
source: This tonic increase in activity was clearly in contrast with the phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition, in which the reward value did not change (right in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a comparison of activity patterns observed in the data, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The example neuron that showed tonic increase in the value-increase condition did not exhibit clear activity modulation as the reward value gradually decreased in the value-decrease condition.
source: This neuron did not exhibit clear activity modulation as the reward value gradually decreased in the value-decrease condition (middle in Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the behavior of a specific neuron across conditions, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Another example dopamine neuron tonically decreased its activity in the value-decrease condition.
source: Another example dopamine neuron tonically decreased its activity in the value-decrease condition (middle in Figure 2B)
evidence: This describes an observation from another single neuron example, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The neuron that showed tonic decrease in the value-decrease condition did not exhibit clear activity modulation in the value-increase condition.
source: but it did not exhibit clear activity modulation in the value-increase condition (left in Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the behavior of a specific neuron across conditions, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The neuron that showed tonic decrease in the value-decrease condition displayed phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition.
source: This neuron also displayed phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition (right in Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the behavior of a specific neuron, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 19 of the 99 dopamine neurons exhibited a significantly positive regression slope between firing rate and time in the value-increase condition.
source: In the value-increase condition, 19 of the 99 dopamine neurons exhibited a significantly positive slope (p<0.05; linear regression analysis)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of the recorded neurons.

claim: On average, the regression slope between firing rate and time was significantly larger than zero in the value-increase condition (n=99 neurons, mean±SD=0.046±0.17, p=0.029).
source: and, on average, the regression slope was significantly larger than zero (n = 99 neurons, mean ± SD = 0.046 ± 0.17, p=0.029; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the population analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The averaged activity of the 19 dopamine neurons with positive slope exhibited a clear tonic increase as the reward value gradually increased.
source: The averaged activity of the 19 dopamine neurons exhibited a clear tonic increase as the reward value gradually increased (left in Figure 2E)
evidence: This describes the averaged activity pattern shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 19 dopamine neurons with tonic increase displayed value-representing phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and value: n=19 neurons, mean±SD=1.61±1.42, p=6.25×10−4).
source: and displayed value-representing phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and value: n = 19 neurons, mean ± SD = 1.61 ± 1.42, p=6.25 × 10−4; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (right in Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the phasic responses of these neurons, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 15 of the 99 dopamine neurons exhibited a significantly negative regression slope between firing rate and time in the value-decrease condition.
source: In the value-decrease condition, 15 of the 99 dopamine neurons exhibited a significantly negative slope (p<0.05; linear regression analysis)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of the recorded neurons.

claim: On average, the regression slope between firing rate and time was significantly smaller than zero in the value-decrease condition (n=99 neurons, mean±SD=−0.048±0.18, p=0.01).
source: and, on average, the regression slope was significantly smaller than zero (n = 99 neurons, mean ± SD = −0.048 ± 0.18, p=0.01; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the population analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The averaged activity of the 15 dopamine neurons with negative slope exhibited a clear tonic decrease as the reward value gradually decreased.
source: The averaged activity of the 15 dopamine neurons exhibited a clear tonic decrease as the reward value gradually decreased (left in Figure 2F)
evidence: This describes the averaged activity pattern shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The 15 dopamine neurons with tonic decrease displayed value-representing phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and value: n=15 neurons, mean±SD=2.10±0.97, p=6.10×10−5).
source: and displayed value-representing phasic responses to the CSs in the value-fixed condition (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and value: n = 15 neurons, mean ± SD = 2.10 ± 0.97, p=6.10 × 10−5; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (right in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the phasic responses of these neurons, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Single dopamine neurons rarely exhibited both tonic increase and decrease in activity in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions, respectively.
source: Notably, single dopamine neurons rarely exhibited both tonic increase and decrease in activity in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions, respectively (no significant correlation between the regression slopes in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions: n = 99 neurons, r = 0.048, p=0.64; correlation analysis) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between tonic increases and decreases, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A subset of dopamine neurons monitored the gradually increasing and decreasing reward values by tonically changing their activity, although the neurons did not signal these values in a unified manner.
source: These results suggest that a subset of dopamine neurons monitored the gradually increasing and decreasing reward values by tonically changing their activity, although the neurons did not signal these values in a unified manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: There was no significant difference in spike width between the time windows for the 19 dopamine neurons with a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition (n=19, spike width during tonic activity: mean±SD=0.32±0.08 ms, spike width during phasic responses: mean±SD=0.33±0.10 ms, p=0.12).
source: There was no significant difference in spike width between the time windows for the 19 dopamine neurons with a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition (n = 19, spike width during the time window to detect the tonic activity increase in the value-increase condition: mean ± SD = 0.32 ± 0.08 ms, spike width during the time window to detect the CS-aligned phasic responses in the value-fixed condition: mean ± SD = 0.33 ± 0.10 ms, p=0.12; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from spike waveform analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There was no significant difference in spike width between the time windows for the 15 dopamine neurons with a tonic decrease in activity in the value-decrease condition (n=15, spike width during tonic activity: mean±SD=0.31±0.07 ms, spike width during phasic responses: mean±SD=0.31±0.06 ms, p=0.53).
source: or for the 15 dopamine neurons with a tonic decrease in activity in the value-decrease condition (n = 15, spike width during the time window to detect the tonic activity decrease in the value-decrease condition: mean ± SD = 0.31 ± 0.07 ms, spike width during the time window to detect the CS-aligned phasic responses in the value-fixed condition: mean ± SD = 0.31 ± 0.06 ms, p=0.53; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from spike waveform analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The tonic increase and decrease in activity were not caused by spikes of non-dopamine neurons contaminating single-unit recording.
source: These results suggest that the tonic increase and decrease in activity were not caused by spikes of non-dopamine neurons contaminating single-unit recording.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spike width analysis showing no differences between time windows.

claim: There was no significant difference in baseline firing rate among the three conditions for the 19 dopamine neurons (n=19, value-increase: mean±SD=3.4±1.2 spikes/s, value-decrease: mean±SD=3.2±1.3 spikes/s, value-fixed: mean±SD=3.6±1.2 spikes/s, p=0.50).
source: On average, these was no significant difference in baseline firing rate among the conditions for the 19 dopamine neurons (n = 19, value-increase condition: mean ± SD = 3.4 ± 1.2 spikes/s, value-decrease condition: mean ± SD = 3.2 ± 1.3 spikes/s, value-fixed condition: mean ± SD = 3.6 ± 1.2 spikes/s, p=0.50; Kruskal-Wallis test)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from baseline firing rate analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in baseline firing rate among the three conditions for the 15 dopamine neurons (n=15, value-increase: mean±SD=3.7±1.0 spikes/s, value-decrease: mean±SD=3.8±1.3 spikes/s, value-fixed: mean±SD=3.8±1.0 spikes/s, p=0.94).
source: or the 15 dopamine neurons (n = 15, value-increase condition: mean ± SD = 3.7 ± 1.0 spikes/s, value-decrease condition: mean ± SD = 3.8 ± 1.3 spikes/s, value-fixed condition: mean ± SD = 3.8 ± 1.0 spikes/s, p=0.94; Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from baseline firing rate analysis.

claim: Only a few neurons (4 of the 19 neurons and 4 of the 15 neurons) exhibited a significant difference in baseline firing among the three conditions.
source: Even at the single-neuron level, only a few neurons (4 of the 19 neurons and 4 of the 15 neurons) exhibited a significant difference in baseline firing among the three conditions (p<0.05; Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from single-neuron analysis.

claim: The three different activity patterns were not due to the loss of spikes or emergence of other spikes during single-unit recording.
source: These results suggest that the three different activity patterns were not due to the loss of spikes or emergence of other spikes during single-unit recording.
evidence: This is an inference based on the baseline firing rate analysis.

claim: The tonic increase and decrease in activity were consistently observed between the first and latter blocks of each condition.
source: Although each condition consisted of a block of 50 trials and was repeated once or more for each recording session (Figure 1D), the tonic increase and decrease in activity were consistently observed between the first and latter blocks of each condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This describes the consistency of the findings across blocks, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: No neuron exhibited a significantly different regression slope between the first and latter blocks.
source: No neuron exhibited a significantly different regression slope between the first and latter blocks (p>0.05; comparison of two regression slopes).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the consistency of neural responses across blocks.

claim: The tonic increase and decrease in activity were consistently observed within each block.
source: Furthermore, the tonic increase and decrease in activity were also consistently observed within each block (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C,D).
evidence: This describes the consistency of the findings within blocks, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C,D.

claim: No neuron exhibited a significantly different regression slope between the first half and latter half trials of blocks.
source: No neuron exhibited a significantly different regression slope between the first half and latter half trials of blocks (p>0.05; comparison of two regression slopes).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the consistency of neural responses within blocks.

claim: The tonic activity changes occurred in consistent manner between and within blocks.
source: These results suggest that the tonic activity changes occurred in consistent manner between and within blocks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency analyses.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibited a tonic increase in activity when future rewards were uncertain, according to a previous study.
source: A previous study reported that dopamine neurons exhibited a tonic increase in activity when future rewards were uncertain (Fiorillo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: The 19 dopamine neurons that exhibited a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition did not exhibit a tonic increase in activity when the CS did not predict the future reward with certainty in the value-fixed condition.
source: Contrary to this assumption, the 19 dopamine neurons, which exhibited a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition, did not exhibit a tonic increase in activity when the CS did not predict the future reward with certainty in the value-fixed condition (dotted curves in the right column of Figure 2E).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the neurons in the uncertain reward condition, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the 19 neurons with tonic increase, the regression slope between firing rate and time in the uncertain reward condition was not significantly different from zero (n=19 neurons, mean±SD=0.015±0.098, p=0.20).
source: On average, the regression slope between firing rate and time was not significantly different from zero (n = 19 neurons, mean ± SD = 0.015 ± 0.098, p=0.20; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about neural activity in the uncertain reward condition.

claim: The tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition was not evoked by uncertainty.
source: This result suggests that the tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition was not evoked by uncertainty.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of activity in different uncertainty conditions.

claim: A subgroup of dopamine neurons increases their activity when animals simply initiate a body movement, according to recent studies using rodents.
source: Recent studies using rodents have shown that a subgroup of dopamine neurons increases their activity when animals simply initiate a body movement (da Silva et al., 2018; Howe and Dombeck, 2016)
evidence: This is a statement about prior research in rodents, supported by citations.

claim: Movement-related dopamine neuron activation has not been reported in primates.
source: although such movement-related dopamine neuron activation has not been reported in primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of certain findings in the primate literature.

claim: The monkeys sporadically licked the spout for reward delivery while the reward value gradually changed.
source: In the present study, we observed that the monkeys sporadically licked the spout for reward delivery while the reward value gradually changed (see Figure 2—figure supplement 6A and C for the value-increase and value-decrease conditions, respectively).
evidence: This describes a behavioral observation, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A and C.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibiting a tonic increase or decrease in activity did not exhibit clear activity modulation around the onset of licking events.
source: These dopamine neurons did not exhibit clear activity modulation around the onset (see Figure 2—figure supplement 6B for the dopamine neurons with a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition, and see Figure 2—figure supplement 6D for the dopamine neurons with a tonic decrease in activity in the value-decrease condition)
evidence: This describes the relationship between neural activity and licking, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B and D.

claim: The tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity were not caused by licking.
source: suggesting that the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity were not caused by licking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of activity modulation around licking events.

claim: The monkeys often made eye movements along the vertical bar stimulus while the reward value gradually changed.
source: We also observed that the monkeys often made eye movements along the vertical bar stimulus (i.e., CS) while the reward value gradually changed (see Figure 2—figure supplement 7A and E for example trials in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions, respectively).
evidence: This describes a behavioral observation, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7A and E.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibiting a tonic increase and decrease in activity did not exhibit clear activity modulation around the onset of saccades.
source: These dopamine neurons did not exhibit clear activity modulation around the onset (see Figure 2—figure supplement 7B for the dopamine neurons with a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition, and see Figure 2—figure supplement 7F for the dopamine neurons with a tonic decrease in activity in the value-decrease condition).
evidence: This describes the relationship between neural activity and saccades, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7B and F.

claim: On average, dopamine neurons with tonic increase or decrease did not exhibit a significant correlation coefficient between firing rate and vertical gaze position in most bins except the bin from 1650 to 1850 ms in the value-increase condition (n=19 neurons, mean±SD=−0.14±0.20, p=0.011).
source: On average, these dopamine neurons did not exhibit a significant correlation coefficient between firing rate and vertical gaze position in either bin except the bin from 1650 to 1850 ms in the value-increase condition (n = 19 neurons, mean ± SD = −0.14 ± 0.20, p=0.011; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis between firing rate and gaze position.

claim: The tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity were not caused by eye movements.
source: These results suggest that the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity were not caused by eye movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between neural activity and eye movements.

claim: An example dopamine neuron phasically decreased its activity when the value stopped increasing in the value-increase condition.
source: An example dopamine neuron phasically decreased its activity when the value stopped increasing in the value-increase condition (left in Figure 3A)
evidence: This describes an observation from a single neuron example, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The example dopamine neuron phasically increased its activity when the value stopped decreasing in the value-decrease condition.
source: and phasically increased its activity when the value stopped decreasing in the value-decrease condition (right in Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes an observation from a single neuron example, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phasic decrease and increase in activity were generally observed across the recorded dopamine neurons when the value stopped changing.
source: Such phasic decrease and increase in activity were generally observed across the recorded dopamine neurons
evidence: This is a generalization based on observations across the population of recorded neurons.

claim: The stopping of the value increase was undesirable and evoked the phasic decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
source: That is, the stopping of the value increase was undesirable and evoked the phasic decrease in dopamine neuron activity
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural responses in terms of conventional dopamine signaling.

claim: The stopping of the value decrease was desirable and evoked the phasic increase in dopamine neuron activity.
source: whereas the stopping of the value decrease was desirable and evoked the phasic increase in dopamine neuron activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural responses in terms of conventional dopamine signaling.

claim: The earlier the reward value stopped increasing (i.e., the smaller the reward value), the more strongly the phasic activity decreased (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and reward value: n=99 neurons, mean±SD=0.31±0.81, p=1.97×10−5).
source: Notably, the earlier the reward value stopped increasing (i.e., the smaller the reward value), the more strongly the phasic activity decreased (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and reward value: n = 99 neurons, mean ± SD = 0.31 ± 0.81, p=1.97 × 10−5; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 3B, also see left in Figure 3C for the averaged activity of 37 dopamine neurons with a significantly positive regression coefficient).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between reward value and phasic activity decrease, shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The earlier the reward value stopped decreasing (i.e., the larger the reward value), the more strongly the phasic activity increased (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and reward value: n=99 neurons, mean±SD=0.59±1.01, p=7.66×10−8).
source: Furthermore, the earlier the reward value stopped decreasing (i.e., the larger the reward value), the more strongly the phasic activity increased (significantly positive regression coefficient between firing rate and reward value: n = 99 neurons, mean ± SD = 0.59 ± 1.01, p=7.66 × 10−8; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 3D, also see right in Figure 3C for the averaged activity of 27 dopamine neurons with a significantly positive regression coefficient).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between reward value and phasic activity increase, shown in Figure 3D and 3C.

claim: The phasic decrease and increase in dopamine neuron activity likely reflected the reward value that was fixed when the green area stopped changing.
source: Thus, the phasic decrease and increase in dopamine neuron activity likely reflected the reward value that was fixed when the green area stopped changing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between phasic activity and reward value.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the regression coefficient for cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition and the regression slope for tonic activity increase in the value-increase condition (n=99 neurons, r=−0.083, p=0.42).
source: Even if dopamine neurons exhibited a cue-aligned phasic activity that represented the value of cued reward in the value-fixed condition, these neurons did not necessarily display a tonic increase in activity (i.e., a positive regression slope between firing rate and time) in the value-increase condition (no significant correlation between the regression coefficient and the regression slope: n = 99 neurons, r = −0.083, p=0.42; correlation analysis) (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between phasic and tonic activities, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the regression coefficient for cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition and the regression slope for tonic activity decrease in the value-decrease condition (n=99 neurons, r=−0.003, p=0.97).
source: or a tonic decrease in activity (i.e., a negative regression slope between firing rate and time) in the value-decrease condition (no significant correlation between the regression coefficient and the regression slope: n = 99 neurons, r = −0.003, p=0.97; correlation analysis) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between phasic and tonic activities, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the regression coefficient for stop-aligned phasic activity decrease in the value-increase condition and the regression slope for tonic activity decrease in the value-decrease condition (n=99 neurons, r=−0.069, p=0.50).
source: Furthermore, even if dopamine neurons exhibited a stop-aligned phasic activity decrease that reflected the reward value in the value-increase condition, these neurons did not necessarily display a tonic decrease in activity (i.e., a negative regression slope between firing rate and time) in the value-decrease condition (no significant correlation between the regression coefficient and the regression slope: n = 99 neurons, r = −0.069, p=0.50; correlation analysis) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between phasic and tonic activities, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no clear relationship between the phasic and tonic activity decreases.
source: Thus, there was no clear relationship between the phasic and tonic activity decreases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between these activity types.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the regression coefficient for stop-aligned phasic activity increase in the value-decrease condition and the regression slope for tonic activity increase in the value-increase condition (n=99 neurons, r=0.061, p=0.55).
source: In addition, even if dopamine neurons exhibited a stop-aligned phasic activity increase that reflected the reward value in the value-decrease condition, these neurons did not necessarily display a tonic increase in activity (i.e., a positive regression slope between firing rate and time) in the value-increase condition (no significant correlation between the regression coefficient and the regression slope: n = 99 neurons, r = 0.061, p=0.55; correlation analysis) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between phasic and tonic activities, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no clear relationship between the phasic and tonic activity increases.
source: Thus, there was no clear relationship between the phasic and tonic activity increases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between these activity types.

claim: The tonic activity tracking the changing reward values was evoked independently of the phasic activity that represents the static, unchanged reward values.
source: Taken together, the above results suggest that the tonic activity tracking the changing reward values was evoked independently of the phasic activity that represents the static, unchanged reward values.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlations between tonic and phasic activities.

claim: The cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition and the stop-aligned phasic activity in the value-increase condition were significantly correlated (n=99 neurons, r=0.48, p=5.6×10−7).
source: These phasic responses were significantly correlated with each other (the regression coefficient for the cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition versus the regression coefficient for the stop-aligned phasic activity decrease in the value-increase condition: Figure 4E, n = 99 neurons, r = 0.48, p=5.6 × 10−7
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between different phasic activities, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition and the stop-aligned phasic activity in the value-decrease condition were significantly correlated (n=99 neurons, r=0.29, p=0.003).
source: the regression coefficient for the cue-aligned phasic activity in the value-fixed condition versus the regression coefficient for the stop-aligned phasic activity increase in the value-decrease condition: Figure 4F, n = 99 neurons, r = 0.29, p=0.003; correlation analysis).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between different phasic activities, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The same dopamine neurons tended to exhibit both of the cue-aligned and stop-aligned phasic activities.
source: Thus, the same dopamine neurons tended to exhibit both of the cue-aligned and stop-aligned phasic activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the significant correlations between these phasic activities.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibit two different firing modes: burst spike firing and non-burst spike firing.
source: Dopamine neurons are known to exhibit two different firing modes: burst spike firing and non-burst spike firing (Grace and Bunney, 1984a; Grace and Bunney, 1984b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dopamine neuron firing modes, supported by citations.

claim: The phasic activity increase of dopamine neurons, which reflects reward prediction errors, is produced by burst spike firing.
source: The phasic activity increase of these neurons, which has been shown to reflect reward prediction errors, is produced by burst spike firing (Bayer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between burst firing and phasic activity, supported by a citation.

claim: Non-burst spike firing in the 19 dopamine neurons with tonic increase increased tonically as the reward value gradually increased.
source: We calculated the averaged activity of the 19 dopamine neurons that exhibited a tonic increase in activity in the value-increase condition separately for burst and non-burst spikes, and found that non-burst spike firing in these neurons increased tonically as the reward value gradually increased (left in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the analysis of burst and non-burst spikes, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Burst spike firing in the 19 dopamine neurons with tonic increase increased when the reward value came close to the maximum value near the end of the value-increase period.
source: On the other hand, burst spike firing in these neurons increased when the reward value came close to the maximum value near the end of the value-increase period.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the analysis of burst spikes.

claim: Non-burst spike firing exhibited a significantly larger firing rate compared with burst spike firing in the initial and middle periods, but there was no significant difference in the late period (initial: p=0.006; middle: p=0.018; late: p=0.43).
source: We found that, while non-burst spike firing exhibited a significantly larger firing rate (original firing rate – baseline firing rate) compared with burst spike firing in the initial and middle periods, there was no significant difference in the late period (initial period: p=0.006; middle period: p=0.018; late period: p=0.43; bootstrap test with 1000 repetitions).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparison of burst and non-burst spike firing across time periods.

claim: The 19 dopamine neurons with tonic increase exhibited a phasic increase in activity only with burst spike firing and not with non-burst spike firing in response to the CS predicting the large reward in the value-fixed condition.
source: Notably, these neurons exhibited a phasic increase in activity only with burst spike firing and not with non-burst spike firing in response to the CS predicting the large reward in the value-fixed condition (right in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the firing mode underlying phasic responses, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The phasic increase in activity evoked when the reward value stopped decreasing in the value-decrease condition was produced only by burst spike firing.
source: In addition, the phasic increase in activity evoked when the reward value stopped decreasing in the value-decrease condition was also produced only by burst spike firing (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the firing mode underlying phasic responses, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: While the conventional phasic activity of dopamine neurons signaling the static, unchanged reward values was evoked by burst spike firing, the tonic activity tracking the changing reward values was produced more largely by non-burst spike firing.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that, while the conventional phasic activity of dopamine neurons signaling the static, unchanged reward values was evoked by burst spike firing, the tonic activity tracking the changing reward values was produced more largely by non-burst spike firing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings about burst and non-burst spike contributions to different activity types.

claim: Recent studies using freely moving rodents reported that dopamine release in the striatum exhibited a tonic increase (or ramp) as animals approached rewards.
source: Although the phasic activity of dopamine neurons has attracted attention for its crucial roles in reward processing, recent studies using freely moving rodents reported that dopamine release in the striatum exhibited a tonic increase (or ramp) as animals approached rewards (Engelhard et al., 2019; Hamid et al., 2016; Howe et al., 2013; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research in rodents, supported by citations.

claim: The tonic increase in dopamine release has not been observed in dopamine neuron spike activity in the VTA.
source: Such tonic increase has not been observed in dopamine neuron spike activity, at least in the VTA (Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of certain findings in prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: The tonic increase in dopamine release has been proposed to represent 'state values' that gradually increase as animals spatially and temporally approach rewards.
source: Although the phasic activity of dopamine neurons has long been thought to represent reward prediction errors, the tonic increase in dopamine release has been proposed to represent 'state values' that gradually increase as animals spatially and temporally approach rewards (Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from prior research, supported by citations.

claim: It is not immediately clear whether the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron spike activity observed in head-fixed monkeys represent state values or reward prediction errors.
source: However, it is not immediately clear whether the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron spike activity, which we observed in head-fixed monkeys, represent state values or reward prediction errors.
evidence: This is a statement about the ambiguity in interpreting the current findings.

claim: Both the state values and reward prediction errors gradually changed in the same fashion in the Pavlovian procedure used in this study.
source: Because both the state values and reward prediction errors gradually changed in the same fashion in our Pavlovian procedure, we were unable to definitely identify which variable the tonic activity of dopamine neurons represented.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The tonic activity occurred independently of the phasic activity that has been thought to represent reward prediction errors.
source: On the other hand, we observed that, even if dopamine neurons exhibited a strong phasic activity, these neurons did not necessarily display a tonic increase or decrease in activity. That is, the tonic activity occurred independently of the phasic activity that has been thought to represent reward prediction errors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between tonic and phasic activities.

claim: The tonic activity might not represent reward prediction errors.
source: This suggests that the tonic activity might not represent reward prediction errors
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the independence of tonic and phasic activities.

claim: Dopamine neurons represent not only reward prediction errors but also multiple signals related to various events and behaviors, including punishments, movements, subjective sensory experience, response inhibition, decision-making, and working memory.
source: and appears to be in accord with a recent perspective that dopamine neurons represent not only reward prediction errors but also multiple signals related to various events and behaviors, including punishments, movements, subjective sensory experience, response inhibition, decision-making, and working memory (Brischoux et al., 2009; da Silva et al., 2018; de Lafuente and Romo, 2011; Engelhard et al., 2019; Howard et al., 2017; Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Menegas et al., 2018; Ogasawara et al., 2018; Yun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about a recent perspective in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The motion of the green area might cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
source: An attribute that might cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity is the motion of the green area. Since the green area dynamically increased and decreased in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions, respectively, in which we observed the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity, it might be possible that these motions of the green area caused the tonic activity changes irrespective of the changing reward value.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed tonic activity.

claim: Dopamine neurons exhibited a phasic activation but not tonic activity change in response to moving-dot images, according to a previous study in monkeys.
source: On the other hand, a previous study in monkeys observed that dopamine neurons exhibited a phasic activation but not tonic activity change in response to moving-dot images (Nomoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: The motion itself was unlikely to cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
source: According to this observation, the motion itself was unlikely to cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research findings.

claim: The time distance to the reward delivery was unlikely to cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
source: However, dopamine neurons exhibited the opposite modulations (i.e., the tonic increase and decrease in activity) in the value-increase and value-decrease conditions in which the time distance to the reward delivery equally became shorter as the green area changed. Therefore, the time distance was also unlikely to cause the tonic increase and decrease in dopamine neuron activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the opposite modulations observed in conditions with similar time distances.

claim: The phasic dopamine activity, which is presumed to represent reward prediction errors, has been considered to provide teaching signals in reinforcement learning.
source: While the phasic dopamine activity, which is presumed to represent reward prediction errors, has been considered to provide teaching signals in reinforcement learning (Doya, 2002; Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997)
evidence: This is a statement about an established theory in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The tonic dopamine activity has been proposed to regulate motivation.
source: the tonic dopamine activity has been proposed to regulate motivation (Cagniard et al., 2006; Niv, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical proposal, supported by citations.

claim: Incentive salience theory proposes that dopamine signals assign incentive values to goals or actions of behavioral processes and motivate actions aimed at acquiring rewards.
source: A theory called 'incentive salience theory' proposes that dopamine signals assign incentive values to goals or actions of behavioral processes and motivate actions aimed at acquiring rewards (Berridge and Robinson, 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical framework, supported by a citation.

claim: The tonic dopamine neuron activity seems to be a good candidate for a neural substrate that regulates the motivational vigor of actions in changing environments in which reward values fluctuate.
source: According to this theory, the tonic dopamine neuron activity, which we observed in the present study, seems to be a good candidate for a neural substrate that regulates the motivational vigor of actions in changing environments in which reward values fluctuate.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of incentive salience theory.

claim: By tracking the changing values of future rewards, the tonic activity might enhance and suppress the motivational vigor of actions to obtain the rewards on a moment-by-moment basis.
source: That is, by tracking the changing values of future rewards, the tonic activity might enhance and suppress the motivational vigor of actions to obtain the rewards on a moment-by-moment basis.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the functional role of tonic dopamine activity.

claim: Instead of phasic firing, tonic firing of dopamine neurons continuously tracked reward values changing moment-by-moment.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrated that, instead of phasic firing, tonic firing of dopamine neurons continuously tracked reward values changing moment-by-moment.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Tonic dopamine activity was produced more largely by non-burst spikes than burst spikes that evoked the phasic dopamine neuron activity.
source: This tonic activity was produced more largely by non-burst spikes than burst spikes that evoked the phasic dopamine neuron activity.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding about the firing modes underlying tonic activity.

claim: The findings expand the current knowledge on dopamine neuron signals by highlighting the alternating firing modes of these neurons, which effectively signal reward values in a given situation.
source: Our findings expand the current knowledge on dopamine neuron signals by highlighting the alternating firing modes of these neurons, which effectively signal reward values in a given situation.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Further investigations are needed to definitely determine whether the tonic activity of dopamine neurons represents state values, reward prediction errors, or other reward-related variables.
source: Further investigations are called for to definitely determine whether the tonic activity of dopamine neurons represents state values, reward prediction errors, or other reward-related variables.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Two adult macaque monkeys (Macaca fuscata; monkey H, female, 6.6 kg, 8 years old; monkey P, female, 6.8 kg, 7 years old) were used for the experiments.
source: Two adult macaque monkeys (Macaca fuscata; monkey H, female, 6.6 kg, 8 years old; monkey P, female, 6.8 kg, 7 years old) were used for the experiments.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All procedures for animal care and experimentation were approved by the University of Tsukuba Animal Experiment Committee (permission number 14–137).
source: All procedures for animal care and experimentation were approved by the University of Tsukuba Animal Experiment Committee (permission number 14–137)
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The procedures were carried out in accordance with the guidelines described in Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the Institute for Laboratory Animal Research.
source: and were carried out in accordance with the guidelines described in Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the Institute for Laboratory Animal Research.
evidence: This describes the ethical guidelines followed in the study.

claim: Behavioral tasks were controlled using MATLAB with Psychtoolbox.
source: Behavioral tasks were controlled using MATLAB (Mathworks, MA) with Psychtoolbox, a freely available toolbox for MATLAB.
evidence: This describes the software used for experimental control.

claim: Eye movements were monitored using an infrared eye-tracking system (EYE-TRAC 6; Applied Science Laboratories, MA) with sampling at 240 Hz.
source: Eye movements were monitored using an infrared eye-tracking system (EYE-TRAC 6; Applied Science Laboratories, MA) with sampling at 240 Hz.
evidence: This describes the equipment and methods used for eye tracking.

claim: Licking of the monkeys was monitored during the recording of 68 of the 99 recorded dopamine neurons.
source: Licking of the monkeys was monitored during the recording of 68 of the 99 recorded dopamine neurons.
evidence: This describes the extent of licking monitoring in the study.

claim: A strain gauge was attached to the spout and measured the strain of the spout caused by licking.
source: To monitor licking, a strain gauge was attached to the spout and measured the strain of the spout caused by licking.
evidence: This describes the method used to monitor licking.

claim: The gradual increase in the value-increase condition randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the onset of the bar stimulus with a uniform distribution from 0 to 2450 ms.
source: The gradual increase randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the onset of the bar stimulus (uniform distribution from 0 to 2450 ms) so that the monkey was unable to precisely predict the reward value until the green area stopped increasing.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The monkey was unable to precisely predict the reward value until the green area stopped increasing in the value-increase condition.
source: The gradual increase randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the onset of the bar stimulus (uniform distribution from 0 to 2450 ms) so that the monkey was unable to precisely predict the reward value until the green area stopped increasing.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the random stopping time in the experimental design.

claim: The gradual decrease in the value-decrease condition randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the bar onset with a uniform distribution from 0 to 2450 ms.
source: The gradual decrease randomly stopped within 2450 ms after the bar onset (uniform distribution from 0 to 2450 ms).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The total time during which the CS was presented was fixed at 2850 ms in each condition.
source: In each condition, the total time during which the CS was presented was fixed at 2850 ms, and the monkey was required to maintain the central fixation during this period.
evidence: This describes a controlled parameter in the experimental design.

claim: The monkey was required to maintain the central fixation during the 2850 ms CS presentation period.
source: In each condition, the total time during which the CS was presented was fixed at 2850 ms, and the monkey was required to maintain the central fixation during this period.
evidence: This describes a behavioral requirement in the experimental procedure.

claim: The reward was delivered simultaneously with a tone (1000 Hz) immediately after the offset of the bar stimulus.
source: Immediately after the offset of the bar stimulus, the reward indicated by the green area was delivered simultaneously with a tone (1000 Hz).
evidence: This describes the timing and method of reward delivery.

claim: The order of the three conditions was fixed across recording sessions: (1) value-fixed, (2) value-increase, and (3) value-decrease.
source: The order of the three conditions, (1) the value-fixed, (2) value-increase, and (3) value-decrease conditions, was fixed across recording sessions.
evidence: This describes the structure of the experimental sessions.

claim: The total amount of reward was the same (10 ml) among blocks.
source: The total amount of reward was the same (10 ml) among blocks.
evidence: This describes a controlled parameter in the experimental design.

claim: Trials were aborted immediately if the monkey did not start the central fixation within 4000 ms after the onset of the fixation point or broke the central fixation during the required fixation period.
source: Trials were aborted immediately if the monkey (1) did not start the central fixation within 4000 ms after the onset of the fixation point or (2) broke the central fixation during the initial 400 ms fixation period or the 2850 ms CS period (i.e., a continuous 3250 ms fixation was required).
evidence: This describes the criteria for trial abortion in the experimental procedure.

claim: Error trials were signaled by a beep tone (100 Hz) and excluded from analyses.
source: These error trials were signaled by a beep tone (100 Hz) and excluded from analyses.
evidence: This describes how error trials were handled in the experimental procedure and analysis.

claim: In the choice task, the monkey was required to choose one of two bar stimuli by making a saccade immediately after the presentation of the bar stimuli.
source: After a 400 ms fixation period, two bar stimuli with red and green areas (2.9°×9.4°) were presented on the right and left sides of the fixation point (eccentricity: 8.8°). The monkey was required to choose one of the bar stimuli by making a saccade immediately after the presentation of the bar stimuli.
evidence: This describes the behavioral requirement in the choice task.

claim: In the choice task, the size of the green area indicated the value of the reward that the monkey would obtain by choosing that bar stimulus and was randomly assigned to each bar stimulus with a uniform distribution from 0.1 to 0.3 ml.
source: The size of the green area indicated the value of the reward that the monkey would obtain by choosing that bar stimulus and was randomly assigned to each bar stimulus (uniform distribution from 0.1 to 0.3 ml).
evidence: This describes how reward values were assigned in the choice task.

claim: Single-unit recordings were performed using tungsten electrodes with impedances of approximately 3.0 MΩ.
source: Single-unit recordings were performed using tungsten electrodes with impedances of approximately 3.0 MΩ (Frederick Haer, ME)
evidence: This describes the equipment used for neural recordings.

claim: Electrophysiological signals were amplified, band-pass filtered (200 Hz to 3 kHz), and stored in a computer at the sampling rate of 24.4 kHz.
source: Electrophysiological signals were amplified, band-pass filtered (200 Hz to 3 kHz; RZ5D, Tucker-Davis Technologies, FL), and stored in a computer at the sampling rate of 24.4 kHz.
evidence: This describes the signal processing methods used in the study.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons were identified based on their low background firing rate at around 5 Hz, a broad spike potential in clear contrast to neighboring neurons with a high background firing rate in the substantia nigra pars reticulata, and a phasic excitation in response to free reward.
source: Putative dopamine neurons were identified based on their well-established electrophysiological signatures: a low background firing rate at around 5 Hz, a broad spike potential in clear contrast to neighboring neurons with a high background firing rate in the substantia nigra pars reticulata (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and a phasic excitation in response to free reward.
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify dopamine neurons, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Each spike was replaced by a Gaussian curve (σ = 15 ms) to calculate spike density functions.
source: To calculate spike density functions (SDFs), each spike was replaced by a Gaussian curve (σ = 15 ms).
evidence: This describes the method used to calculate spike density functions.

claim: The burst and non-burst spike firing modes were identified based on interspike intervals using previously established criteria.
source: The burst and non-burst spike firing modes were identified based on interspike intervals (ISIs) using previously established criteria (Grace and Bunney, 1984a).
evidence: This describes the method used to identify firing modes, with reference to established criteria.

claim: The criteria for identifying burst spike firing mode were: (1) an ISI of 80 ms or less to identify the onset of the burst spike firing mode and (2) an ISI of more than 160 ms to identify the end of the firing mode.
source: These criteria were (1) an ISI of 80 ms or less to identify the onset of the burst spike firing mode and (2) an ISI of more than 160 ms to identify the end of the firing mode.
evidence: This describes the specific criteria used to identify burst firing.
